item.title: Self-Portrait
item.museum: National Gallery of Art, Washington, D.C.
item.lesson: A young painter spins around mid-brushstroke to chat with you, arm slung over the chair back, mouth open in conversation. The informality is the point — and it is calculated. Judith Leyster was one of the first women admitted as a master to the painters' guild of Haarlem, running her own workshop with students in her early twenties, and this self-portrait is her advertisement: relaxed pose to show her social ease, a laughing fiddler on the easel to show her specialty in lively genre scenes, and virtuoso lace and satin to show what your money buys. After her death she vanished from history — her works were sold as Frans Hals for two centuries, some bearing forged signatures over her own monogram. Only in 1893 did a lawsuit over a misattributed 'Hals' lead scholars back to her distinctive mark: a J and L entwined with a shooting star — a pun on her name, 'lodestar.'
item.lookFor: The fiddler on her easel was originally a girl's face — she painted her sales pitch over an earlier composition, and X-rays caught the revision.
